ask.changes_what: Positive: treat as significant volume loss - IV access, fluid/blood, search for bleeding source; negative: does not exclude moderate haemorrhage, use labs/other findings.
ask.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is already hypotensive, in shock, or with suspected unstable spine/pelvic injury.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not attempt standing in patients who are hypotensive supine, obtunded, or at high fall risk; do not apply the volunteer-derived numbers uncritically to elderly patients on antihypertensives, beta-blockers or with autonomic neuropathy.
ask.escalation_warning: Inability to stand because of dizziness in a patient with suspected bleeding indicates large-volume loss: obtain large-bore access, type and crossmatch, and escalate immediately.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (pooled RCE analysis of postural vital-sign studies)
evidence.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of blood removed by phlebotomy (before vs after)
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolaemia from LARGE acute blood loss (630-1150 mL) - finding: severe postural dizziness (preventing upright vitals) OR postural pulse increment >=30/min

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (pooled RCE analysis of postural vital-sign studies)
evidence.quote: The presence of either finding has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of blood removed by phlebotomy (before vs after)
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolaemia from MODERATE acute blood loss (450-630 mL) - finding: severe postural dizziness OR postural pulse increment >=30/min

ask.how: After supine vitals, stand the patient (with assistance) and ask about dizziness while measuring pulse and BP at about 1 minute. 'Severe' means dizziness so marked the patient cannot stay standing long enough for upright vitals or nearly faints; record it as a positive finding in its own right, together with any pulse increment of 30/min or more.
ask.negative_finding: Absence is reassuring only against large blood loss (sensitivity 0.97); after moderate (450-630 mL) loss the finding is usually absent (sensitivity 0.22), so a negative test does not exclude clinically important haemorrhage.
ask.pitfalls: Mild postural dizziness has no proven diagnostic value; supine tachycardia or hypotension is often absent even after 1 L loss. Evidence comes from healthy volunteers after phlebotomy, not from elderly or medicated ED patients, in whom baseline orthostatic symptoms are common.
ask.positive_finding: Severe postural dizziness (or a postural pulse increment >=30/min) is highly specific (0.98) for hypovolaemia from blood loss and is present in almost all subjects after large (630-1150 mL) blood loss.
ask.prerequisites: Supine rest for at least 2 minutes before standing; an assistant to prevent a fall. Sitting is not an adequate substitute for standing.
ask.rationale: If the patient is too dizzy to stand, this is a strong indicator of significant volume loss and guides urgent management.
ask.title: Severe postural dizziness / inability to stand for vitals

ask.changes_what: Positive: hold/adjust the culprit, check orthostatic vitals, ECG, creatinine and electrolytes; negative: pursue arrhythmic, structural, vasovagal or infectious causes.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not accept a medication explanation as final in patients with exertional syncope, syncope while supine, palpitations preceding syncope, known structural heart disease or an abnormal ECG.
ask.escalation_warning: Bradycardia or high-grade AV block, QT prolongation, symptomatic hypotension with AKI, or opioid/sedative toxicity with reduced consciousness need monitored care and antidote/withdrawal decisions.
ask.how: Reconcile every drug (prescribed, OTC, herbal, recreational) against the pharmacy list: antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates, alpha-blockers, PDE5 inhibitors, rate-slowing agents (beta-blockers, non-DHP CCB, digoxin), QT-prolonging drugs, sedatives/opioids, psychotropics, insulin/sulfonylureas, NSAIDs/ACEi/ARB/SGLT2i. Note start dates, dose changes and timing of the last dose versus the event.
ask.negative_finding: No culprit drug or no temporal relationship lowers the probability of medication effect but does not exclude intrinsic cardiac or neurological causes.
ask.pitfalls: Patients omit over-the-counter, recreational and 'as needed' drugs; drug effects are amplified by age, renal impairment, volume depletion and drug-drug interactions, so a long-standing drug can still be the cause after a change elsewhere. Attributing syncope to drugs without ECG review can miss conduction disease unmasked by the drug.
ask.positive_finding: A new or up-titrated vasoactive, rate-slowing, sedative or diuretic drug (or an intercurrent illness reducing intake/clearance) temporally linked to the event supports drug-induced orthostatic hypotension, bradyarrhythmia, hypovolemia/AKI or delirium.
ask.prerequisites: Access to an accurate medication list (pharmacy fill data, carer, containers); ask specifically about new drugs and dose escalations within the past 2-4 weeks.
ask.rationale: Recent medication changes or antihypertensive use can directly cause orthostatic symptoms and may require immediate adjustment.
ask.title: Antihypertensive / sedative / new-medication review (timing of last doses)

ask.changes_what: Determines which bedside exam follows: HINTS for continuous spontaneous, Dix-Hallpike for triggered episodic, orthostatic vitals for standing-triggered, ECG/monitoring for spontaneous episodic.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use a reassuring timing/trigger pattern alone to exclude stroke in patients with vascular risk factors, new headache/neck pain, or any brainstem symptom; obtain the targeted examination.
ask.escalation_warning: Acute continuous dizziness with any of diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, limb ataxia, new deafness or inability to walk unaided is a stroke pathway until proven otherwise; up to 20% of early DWI-MRI are false negative.

evidence.citation: Herr RD, Zun L, Mathews JJ. A directed approach to the dizzy patient. Ann Emerg Med. 1989;18(6):664-672.
evidence.population: 125 ED patients with dizziness evaluated with a standardized 66-item history/exam/lab protocol
evidence.quote: The best predictors, either older age, lack of vertigo, or neurologic deficit, could identify 86% of "serious" dizziness with 42% specificity.
evidence.reference_standard: Emergency physician diagnosis modified by 1-month follow-up using predefined diagnostic criteria
evidence.target_condition: 'Serious' cause of dizziness (stroke/TIA, arrhythmia, medication, seizure, other requiring admission) - composite predictor: older age OR lack of vertigo OR neurologic deficit

ask.how: Instead of asking 'what kind of dizziness', ask: Is it there now continuously or does it come in discrete episodes? How long do episodes last (seconds, minutes, hours)? Is it brought on only by a trigger (head/position change, standing) or does it arise spontaneously? Then ask about diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, new hearing loss, headache or neck pain.
ask.negative_finding: A clear positional trigger with seconds-long episodes and no neurologic symptoms makes central causes unlikely, but isolated dizziness can still be a vertebrobasilar stroke.
ask.pitfalls: Symptom-quality descriptors (vertigo vs lightheadedness) are unreliable: 52% of ED patients changed their descriptor on retest after ~6 minutes, so do not triage on 'type'. Do not confuse 'worse with movement' (most vestibular causes) with 'only occurs with movement' (true trigger).
ask.positive_finding: Continuous acute vestibular syndrome demands HINTS-type eye examination for stroke; triggered brief episodes point to BPPV or orthostatic hypotension (test with Dix-Hallpike or orthostatic vitals); spontaneous episodes lasting minutes-hours suggest TIA, Meniere or arrhythmia. Any associated brainstem symptom raises stroke probability.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give a history; screen for red-flag neurologic symptoms before deciding on examination pathway.
ask.rationale: Clarifying the timing and triggers helps distinguish orthostatic from other causes of syncope and guides the next diagnostic step.
ask.title: Timing and triggers (TiTrATE: episodic vs continuous, triggered vs spontaneous) rather than symptom quality; associated diplopia/dysarthria/dysphagia/hearing loss

examine.changes_what: Positive: treat as significant hypovolemia/bleeding or medication-related OH and act; negative: large blood loss unlikely, but moderate loss still possible.
examine.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is frankly hypotensive, has an unstable spine/pelvis, or cannot safely bear weight.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not attempt standing measurements in a patient who is already hypotensive, too dizzy or weak to stand safely, or has an unstable spine or pelvis; a patient too dizzy to stand counts as a positive test.
examine.escalation_warning: A positive test in a patient with possible bleeding indicates large volume loss and should trigger resuscitation and source search, not observation.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)
evidence.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)
evidence.target_condition: Large acute blood loss (630-1150 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)

evidence.target_condition: Moderate acute blood loss (450-630 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy
evidence.quote: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent, even after up to 1150 mL of blood loss (sensitivity, 33%; 95% CI, 21%-47%, for supine hypotension)
evidence.target_condition: Blood loss up to 1150 mL - supine hypotension (comparator finding, not postural)

examine.how: Measure BP and pulse after >=2 min supine, then have the patient stand and repeat at 1 and 3 min (standing, not sitting). Record SBP fall >=20 or DBP fall >=10 mmHg, pulse rise >=30/min, and whether the patient is too dizzy to stand (count that as positive).
examine.negative_finding: A normal postural pulse response argues strongly against large blood loss (LR- about 0.03) but misses most moderate (450-630 mL) losses (sensitivity 22%). Normal orthostatics do not exclude hypovolemia from vomiting/diarrhea.
examine.pitfalls: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent even after 1 L blood loss. Beta-blockers blunt the pulse response; sitting instead of standing lowers sensitivity; mild postural dizziness alone has no proven value.
examine.positive_finding: A postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness is highly specific (98%) for blood loss and is nearly always present after large (>1 L) hemorrhage. In an older patient with syncope, an SBP fall >=20 mmHg reproducing symptoms supports orthostatic hypotension, though asymptomatic falls are common with age and medications.
examine.prerequisites: Automated or manual cuff, an assistant to steady the patient, supine rest of at least 2 minutes first.
examine.rationale: Orthostatic vitals are critical to confirm orthostatic hypotension and guide immediate management decisions.
examine.title: Orthostatic vitals: SBP drop >=20 / DBP >=10 mmHg or pulse increment >=30/min at 1-3 min standing

examine.changes_what: SBP <90/MAP <65: resuscitate, lactate, POCUS (RUSH) to classify shock type, cause-directed therapy now. Normal BP: keep looking for compensated shock (HR, lactate, mentation, urine output).
examine.contraindications: Avoid the arm with a dialysis fistula, lymphoedema or recent axillary surgery; none otherwise.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a single normal cuff reading to exclude shock or tamponade; do not interpret SBP <90 as 'baseline' without documented prior values.
examine.escalation_warning: SBP <90 or MAP <65 with altered mentation, lactate >2, oliguria or cool skin is shock: immediate resuscitation and senior/ICU review; in suspected dissection or tamponade, hypotension signals imminent collapse.

evidence.citation: Ohle R, Kareemi HK, Wells G, Perry JJ. Clinical examination for acute aortic dissection: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2019.
evidence.population: Pooled 4 studies of ED patients evaluated for suspected acute aortic dissection (review total 9 studies, 2,400 participants; prevalence range 21.9-76.1%)
evidence.reference_standard: Acute aortic dissection confirmed by imaging, surgery or autopsy per primary studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute aortic dissection; finding = hypotension as defined by each primary study (thresholds varied; not uniformly SBP <90 mmHg)

evidence.citation: Drazner MH, Hellkamp AS, Leier CV, Shah MR, Miller LW, Russell SD, Young JB, Califf RM, et al. Value of clinician assessment of hemodynamics in advanced heart failure: the ESCAPE trial. Circ Heart Fail. 2009.
evidence.location: Table 5 (Utility of history and physical examination in detecting an invasively measured cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2); columns frequency, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, LR+, LR-, OR, P
evidence.population: 188 patients hospitalised with advanced decompensated HF in the ESCAPE trial with pulmonary artery catheter measurements
evidence.reference_standard: Invasively measured cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2 by pulmonary artery catheter
evidence.target_condition: Low cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2 in advanced heart failure; finding = SBP <90 mmHg on baseline examination

evidence.citation: Guberman BA, Fowler NO, Engel PJ, Gueron M, Allen JM. Cardiac tamponade in medical patients. Circulation. 1981.
evidence.population: 56 medical patients with cardiac tamponade, single-centre case series, University of Cincinnati
evidence.quote: heart sounds were diminished in 19 patients; arterial systolic pressure was greater than or equal to 100 mm Hg in 35
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical/haemodynamic diagnosis of tamponade with relief by pericardiocentesis or pericardial resection
evidence.target_condition: Cardiac tamponade (sensitivity only); finding = systolic BP <100 mmHg (threshold differs from id title's <90)

examine.how: Measure with a correctly sized cuff on a supported arm (manual if the automated reading is doubtful or the pulse is irregular), repeat, and measure both arms when dissection is possible; calculate MAP = (SBP + 2 x DBP)/3. Interpret against the patient's usual pressure and drug list.
examine.negative_finding: A normal SBP does not exclude shock (compensated haemorrhage, early sepsis, cardiogenic shock with vasoconstriction) or tamponade (about 60% of tamponade patients had SBP ≥100), nor low cardiac index in heart failure (SBP <90 sensitivity 12%).
examine.pitfalls: Chronic hypertensives are hypoperfused at 'normal' pressures; beta-blockers, pacemakers and automated cuffs in AF mislead. Interarm difference >20 mmHg raises dissection concern. Cuff readings overestimate true pressure in profound vasoconstriction.
examine.positive_finding: SBP <90 (or MAP <65) is shock until proven otherwise and should trigger a search for the cause (septic, hypovolaemic/haemorrhagic, cardiogenic, obstructive: tamponade/PE/tension pneumothorax, anaphylaxis, adrenal). In suspected dissection, hypotension roughly triples the odds (LR+ 2.9, specificity 95%). It is not a discriminator between causes.
examine.prerequisites: Appropriate cuff size; awareness of baseline BP, beta-blockers/antihypertensives and pacing.
examine.rationale: Detecting hypotension at the bedside prompts urgent resuscitation and changes the safety of further testing.
examine.title: Systolic BP <90 mmHg (or MAP <65) at the bedside

examine.changes_what: Pallor present: check haemoglobin and look for a bleeding source; pallor absent: do not use to exclude anaemia or occult haemorrhage in a symptomatic patient.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of pallor to exclude acute haemorrhage or anaemia in a patient with syncope, hypotension or chest pain - measure haemoglobin.
examine.escalation_warning: Pallor with tachycardia, hypotension or melaena = suspect haemorrhagic shock; obtain access, haemoglobin and cross-match immediately.

evidence.citation: Sheth TN, Choudhry NK, Bowes M, Detsky AS. The relation of conjunctival pallor to the presence of anemia. J Gen Intern Med. 1997.
evidence.population: 302 medical and surgical inpatients, tertiary-care university teaching hospital (prospective, blinded observers)
evidence.quote: LR 4.49 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.80, 10.99); pallor borderline, LR 1.80 (95% CI 1.18, 2.62); pallor absent, LR 0.61 (95% CI 0.44, 0.80)

evidence.citation: Kalantri A, Karambelkar M, Joshi R, Kalantri S, Jajoo U. Accuracy and reliability of pallor for detecting anaemia: a hospital-based diagnostic accuracy study. PLoS One. 2010.
evidence.location: Table 2 (PMC full text), conjunctiva rows; columns Hb <7, <9, <12 g/dL
evidence.population: 390 consecutive outpatient and medicine-inpatient adults >12 y, teaching hospital, rural India (prospective, blinded)
evidence.reference_standard: Haemoglobin by electronic cell counter within 1 day
evidence.target_condition: Anaemia, haemoglobin <9 g/dL (conjunctival pallor graded severe vs none)

evidence.citation: Kalantri A, Karambelkar M, Joshi R, Kalantri S, Jajoo U. Accuracy and reliability of pallor for detecting anaemia: a hospital-based diagnostic accuracy study. PLoS One. 2010.
evidence.location: Table 2 (PMC full text), conjunctiva 'Severe' row, Hb <7 g/dL column
evidence.population: Same 390 patients, teaching hospital, rural India
evidence.reference_standard: Haemoglobin by electronic cell counter within 1 day
evidence.target_condition: Severe anaemia, haemoglobin <7 g/dL (conjunctival pallor graded severe)

examine.how: In good light, gently pull down the lower eyelid and compare the colour of the anterior rim of the palpebral conjunctiva with the deeper posterior conjunctiva: pallor is present when the anterior rim is as pale as the posterior part, borderline when indeterminate. Also inspect palmar creases with the hand extended and the nail beds.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of pallor only modestly lowers the probability of severe anaemia (LR about 0.6) and does not rule it out; it says nothing about acute haemorrhage before haemodilution.
examine.pitfalls: Agreement between examiners ranges from good with explicit criteria to near chance; conjunctivitis, icterus, dark skin and poor lighting mislead. Palmar-crease and nail-bed pallor add little.
examine.positive_finding: Definite conjunctival pallor roughly quadruples the odds of severe anaemia (Hb <=90 g/L, LR about 4.5) and warrants a haemoglobin measurement even without other clues.
examine.prerequisites: Adequate lighting; examiner blinded to haemoglobin if possible.
examine.rationale: Pallor suggests anemia or blood loss, supporting hypovolemia as a cause of syncope.
examine.title: Conjunctival rim pallor (and palmar crease / nail-bed pallor)

examine.changes_what: Elevated JVP moves dyspnea/edema toward acute HF or RV/pericardial disease and away from hypovolemia; a flat JVP in hypotension favors hypovolemia/sepsis over cardiogenic causes.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid firm neck pressure in patients with carotid disease.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal JVP to withhold treatment for suspected heart failure, or declare a shocked patient hypovolemic when the neck cannot be adequately examined (obesity, short neck, column above the jaw).
examine.escalation_warning: Elevated JVP with hypotension, clear lungs and tachycardia suggests tamponade, RV infarction or massive PE and needs immediate echo/POCUS rather than diuresis.

evidence.citation: Butman SM, Ewy GA, Standen JR, Kern KB, Hahn E. Bedside cardiovascular examination in patients with severe chronic heart failure: importance of rest or inducible jugular venous distension. J Am Coll Cardiol 1993;22(4):968-74.
evidence.population: 52 patients with severe chronic heart failure undergoing in-hospital transplant evaluation; index finding = jugular venous distension at rest OR inducible by the abdominojugular test
evidence.quote: had the best combination of sensitivity (81%), specificity (80%) and predictive accuracy (81%) for elevation of the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
evidence.target_condition: Elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (>=18 mmHg)

evidence.citation: Signs and symptoms in adult patients with acute dyspnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Emerg Med 2018;25(1):3-11 (author list not retrievable via abstract tool; confirmed by PMID/DOI).
evidence.population: Adults with a new episode of acute dyspnea; 8 ED studies, 4737 patients; HF prevalence 25-59%
evidence.quote: Elevated jugular venous pressure (0.88, pooled odds ratio: 7), added third heart sound (0.97), and lung crepitations (0.77, pooled odds ratio: 11)
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of HF per included studies (varied)
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure as cause of acute dyspnea

evidence.citation: Mant J, Doust J, Roalfe A, et al. Systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis of diagnosis of heart failure, with modelling of implications of different diagnostic strategies in primary care. Health Technol Assess 2009;13(32):1-207.
evidence.population: Patients with suspected heart failure in primary care; individual patient data meta-analysis of 9 studies
evidence.quote: orthopnoea (89%), oedema (72%), elevated jugular venous pressure (70%), cardiomegaly (85%), added heart sounds (99%), lung crepitations (81%)
evidence.reference_standard: Echocardiography / expert panel per included studies
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure (new diagnosis) in primary care

examine.how: Recline the patient at 30-45 degrees (adjust until the top of the pulsation is visible), turn the head slightly left, and use tangential light to find the top of the internal jugular column. Measure its vertical height above the sternal angle; >3 cm above the angle (about >8 cm H2O total) is elevated.
examine.negative_finding: A flat or normal JVP lowers but does not exclude heart failure; sensitivity is modest (roughly 0.2-0.7 across ED studies) and pooled sensitivity in ED series stays below 0.55.
examine.pitfalls: Confusing carotid with venous pulsation, misjudging the sternal angle-to-atrium distance (varies with position), and failing to see a very high column (look for earlobe pulsation) or a very low one (lie the patient flatter). Isolated RV failure, tricuspid disease, tamponade or constriction raise JVP without left-sided congestion.
examine.positive_finding: A venous column >3 cm above the sternal angle indicates raised right atrial pressure and, in chronic heart failure, usually raised left-sided filling pressure (PCWP >=18 mmHg). It substantially raises the probability of heart failure as the cause of acute dyspnea.
examine.prerequisites: Adequate light, exposed neck, patient relaxed and breathing quietly; identify the venous (biphasic, non-palpable, falls with inspiration, occludable) rather than carotid pulsation.
examine.rationale: JVP assessment helps distinguish hypovolemia from cardiogenic or obstructive causes of syncope.
examine.title: Jugular venous pressure elevated (>8 cm H2O / >3 cm above sternal angle); low/flat JVP as the negative
